name: Nikhil Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the crew putting up timber frames and repairing rough work on building sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and people call me when a frame will not sit square, but my pay is low for a lead. I prefer showing an apprentice the corner with a square in hand to explaining it through a phone, and I have never used AI. My wife Noor and I have two school-age children, a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved. There are few other contractors nearby, so a gap between projects already makes me watch each pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the office can shorten its forms, but a carpenter still has to check the frame before covering it. No software will pay for a wall built out of square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This plateau leaves the trade alone, yet I am already worried about a project gap. A week without paid site work would put the mortgage into the money we need for food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking framing shifts and record the measured corners on the job sheet. After each payday I would put a small amount into an emergency fund only if mortgage and groceries have cleared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, as I am now when one project is nearly finished. The AI story does not create that worry, but it does not settle it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor and I might put twenty away from a full week of pay. On a short week there might be nothing, and I would not call the present balance a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which corner do you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first frame at the stairwell, because one crooked corner throws off the next run of boards. I would make the apprentice measure both diagonals before covering it.

say: **Carpenters** still check every timber frame before covering it, even if the office shortens forms.
**Software forms** cannot correct a crooked wall.
think: A **project gap** could already leave the mortgage short.
Our **thin savings** give almost no cover for a missed week.
do: **Keep** taking framing shifts and measuring corners on site.
**Save** twenty from a full paid week only after mortgage and food clear.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary project gaps even with little AI change.
S0.quote: No software will pay for a wall built out of square.
fieldNote: His **lead skill** coexists with lower pay, less than a month saved and scarce nearby contractors.
His **new saving** would come from future full weeks only after essential bills.

steps.text: Keep framing shifts and measure corners on site
Save twenty from full paid weeks only after mortgage and food clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can speed booking and buying before machines do the hands-on framing. I want the site manager to count real cutting and fitting time before a screen shortens our schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A planner who assumes every wall is straight could squeeze paid hours from my crew. With little saved and few jobs nearby, even a small drop in site pay would reach our mortgage quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would log six framing jobs, including material delays and rework, then show the times to my manager. In the first year Noor and I would stop weekend trips if the new schedule actually cut my paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and angry at a number made without a site visit. I would rather be paid to fix the wall than argue afterward about why it took longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What rework would the schedule miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bowed stud can be found only after the pack is opened, then the replacement has to be cut. I would put that wait beside the fitting time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for another firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a posted local framing job offered steadier paid hours and enough wage for our bills, I would apply. I cannot leave the current site because a future schedule might be wrong.

say: **Booking and buying** change before capable robots can take over hands-on timber framing on sites.
**Real fitting time** belongs in site schedules.
think: Tight **paid hours** could shrink my own site income.
Our **small reserve** and few local jobs make a modest cut serious.
do: **Log** six actual framing jobs with material delays and rework before accepting shorter paid hours.
**Stop** weekend trips if schedule cuts paid hours.
feel: **Anxious** about a short pay slip and weak local fallback.
S1.quote: A planner who assumes every wall is straight could squeeze paid hours from my crew.
fieldNote: He ties **AI scheduling** to a realistic loss of his own paid time.
His **job search** requires a posted local role with steady hours and sufficient wage, not a speculative enquiry.

steps.text: Stop weekend trips if site schedule cuts paid hours
Apply for posted local framing job only if hours steadier and wage covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices thinking AI by 2028 changes plans and buying first, while capable robots for framing arrive around 2031. We still have about three years when the site needs our hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our contractor to cut most of the framing crew once a machine can build a wall for less. With less than a month saved, a mortgage and few local jobs, a big loss of paid shifts would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the manager for the actual crew plan and cut spending on anything beyond bills and food now. If robots cut shifts after 2031, I would apply for a posted local building repair job only if its pay covers our household bills; I would not spend savings on a course without a real vacancy and paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have lain awake counting how many full weeks of framing wages the mortgage needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes from the budget first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor and I would cancel meals out and put off replacing the sofa. The children’s school costs and mortgage would come before either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no repair vacancy locally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep asking nearby contractors about posted work while we still had framing shifts. I would not promise the children a move without a real offer and enough pay.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches plans before capable framing robots around 2031.
**Hands-on framing** remains during the three-year gap.
think: I expect a major cut in **crew shifts** after robots arrive.
The **mortgage and tiny reserve** make a long search frightening.
do: **Cut** meals out and delay the sofa before nonessential spending.
**Apply** after 2031 for posted local repair only if pay covers household bills.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over expected wage loss.
S2.quote: I have lain awake counting how many full weeks of framing wages the mortgage needs.
fieldNote: He expects a **major shift cut**, making alarm fit despite the later robot date.
He rejects **speculative training** without a real vacancy and paid time.

steps.text: Cancel meals out and delay sofa while preparing for 2031 shift loss
Apply after 2031 shift cuts for posted local repairs only if pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us time to see a robot on an uneven site before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Full hands-on robots come around 2034, so the crew should demand a real trial before anyone reduces shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be near fifty when capable machines arrive, with children growing and a mortgage probably still due. I could learn a different site task if a firm paid for it. A course without a building-site wage is no plan for our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a hands-on robot trial and the contractor’s written plan for paid site jobs. If a posted local quality-checking job offers paid training and a wage that covers our bills, I would take the course before 2031 and apply after 2031; otherwise I would keep framing while work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years gives us a chance to see actual jobs rather than guesses. I would still count every pay week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot should frame a wall with a bowed stud and show who decides to reject it. A level demonstration floor would prove little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower wage to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it still covered the mortgage, school and food bills. Noor and I cannot use savings every month to make a new title look workable.

say: **Uneven-site trials** should come before capable building robots can frame walls around 2034.
**Written paid jobs** matter more than general promises.
think: I may need **different site work** near fifty.
A course without **bill-covering pay** cannot protect the mortgage and our children’s ordinary needs.
do: **Request** a hands-on trial and written paid job plan.
**Take** funded quality training for posted local bill-covering vacancy.
**Apply** after 2031 if trained and the posted local wage covers bills.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to check actual options.
S3.quote: A course without a building-site wage is no plan for our mortgage.
fieldNote: His **training and application** both require a posted local role, paid time and enough wage.
He wants an **uneven-site trial** rather than a clean demonstration before judging robots.

steps.text: Take funded quality course for posted local bill-covering vacancy
Apply after 2031 for posted local quality role if trained and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and capable building robots around 2039. I would use the years to build a bigger reserve if our wages allow, because our children may still need help starting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be in my fifties when full site robots arrive, with years of work still ahead. The extra time helps, but it does not guarantee another local contractor or erase the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading framing work and add fifty from each full pay cheque to savings if the household bills are covered. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for a posted local site-maintenance role only if the pay covers our bills and any required training is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but less trapped than in the fast picture. I would like ten years in which to make our bank balance less fragile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the fifty come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From wages on a full week, after the mortgage and food. A short carpentry pay week would add nothing to savings before the mortgage is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children join the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach them to use a square if they wanted. I would not tell them any trade is guaranteed forever, even though ours has fed the family.

say: **2036 thinking AI** precedes capable building robots around 2039.
**Children** may still need help with first adult expenses.
think: More years allow **new savings** from full pay weeks.
Few **local contractors** and the mortgage remain real limits.
do: **Keep** leading framing work on current sites.
**Save** fifty from full pay cheques only after household bills.
**Apply** after 2036 for posted local maintenance only with bill-covering pay and paid training.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to build a less fragile reserve.
S4.quote: A short carpentry pay week would add nothing to savings before the mortgage is paid.
fieldNote: His **fifty-per-cheque plan** is new saving from wages, not money already held.
His **later application** retains posted local work, adequate wages and paid training as conditions.

steps.text: Keep leading framing on current building sites
Save fifty from full pay cheques only after bills
Apply after 2036 for posted local maintenance only with bill-covering pay and paid training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because framing robots around 2031 could take most of our shifts while the mortgage and school bills remain. A real posted local repair job with paid training and bill-covering wages would help more than a promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what a worker does when a robot frame looks square but is not. I want the apprentice to put a level on the robot frame before anyone hangs a door.

portrait: **Nikhil Farah**, 43, leads building-site framing and has a vocational trade certificate.
He and wife Noor have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, lower pay and less than a month saved.
He has **never used AI** and trusts apprenticeships, levels and actual site work over new screens.
In **Steady Disruption**, he expects paid hours could shrink and cuts trips if schedules actually reduce wages.
The **2028 picture** alarms him because he expects a major crew reduction with few local fallbacks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most framing shifts around 2031 while mortgage and school bills continue.
whatWouldHelp: A posted **local repair job** with paid training and bill-covering wages would protect household income.
headlineQuote: I want the apprentice to put a level on the robot frame before anyone hangs a door.
